newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China insists HK leadership race is representive.
newsitem.headline: China insists HK leadership race is representive.

text.p: The pro-Beijing camp in Hong Kong has defended as genuinely representative China's methods for choosing the territory's leaders when British rule ends next year.

"China, while resuming its sovereign rights over Hong Kong, has also given the people of Hong Kong the opportunity for democratic participation in government," said the Beijing-funded Ta Kung Pao newspaper on Monday.
The newspaper echoed comments on Sunday by China's envoy to Hong Kong, Zhang Junshen, and a long commentary carried by China's official Xinhua news agency.
Hong Kong's vocal pro-democracy lobby, largely excluded from the process, has denounced the selection procedure as a sham.
With 239 days to go before the British colony reverts to China, a Beijing-appointed Preparatory Committee is assembling Hong Kong's future government.
On Saturday, it voted in a 400-strong Selection Committee of Hong Kong citizens charged with choosing the territory's first post-colonial leader and a controversial appointed legislature.
The chief executive will take over from Chris Patten, the 28th and last British governor of Hong Kong, when the colony is handed back to China at midnight next June 30.
Four candidates are seen as frontrunners.

Two are wealthy businessmen: Tung Chee-hwa, 59, and Peter Woo, at 50 the youngest candidate. Two are former judges: Simon Li, at 74 the oldest candidate, and Ti Liang Yang, 67, the only member of the quartet not on the Preparatory Committee.
Even the staunchest democrats in Hong Kong admit the process is more participatory than seen in a century and a half of British colonial rule.
"Hard to argue with that," said independent democratic politician Christine Loh. Britain appointed all its governors.
But political analysts and politicians said China's methods showed Beijing wanted to paint their methods as democratic while maintaining control over the outcome.
"It is clear that Beijing had several layers of screening to safeguard the final results," said Loh.

The Preparatory Committee itself screened out more than 5,700 applications to the Selection Committee, submitting a short-list of 408 names for 340 places. Sixty seats were reserved for Hong Kong advisers to China.

Hong Kong's largest pro-Beijing political party, the Democratic Alliance for the Betterment of Hong Kong, which fared poorly in Hong Kong's legislative elections last year, accounted for one in four of the seats on the committee.

Hong Kong's most popular party, the Democrats, which enjoyed the greatest support in the September elections, boycotted the process as undemocratic. Two members of an allied pro-democracy party managed to win places in a committee overwhelmingly dominated by Hong Kong's big business lobby.

"The fact these Selection Committee members were handpicked by the Preparatory Committee shows that there seems to be a list prepared by the Chinese government," said political scientist Sonny Lo of the 1997 Transition Project, a long-term academic study into the changeover.
The domination of the business sector, although ridden with factional rivalries, should lead to a victory for frontrunner businessman candidate Tung, he said.
Woo's youth and lack of political contacts in China mitigate him, political analysts say.
"I think the question is whether Mr Tung will win this election in the first ballot or in the second ballot," said Lo.
